vectors.reason: Unauthorized access to a physical workstation puts the attacker inside the mission's own ground systems.

vectors.enisa_quote: machinery in production/assembly facilities or launch facility
vectors.reason: Machinery in production, assembly and launch facilities belongs to the manufacture and integration phase, which the supply_chain origin models.

notes: Entry-only by design: ENISA names no concrete outcome ('multitude of nefarious activities'), so no impact or exfiltration is kept and no scenario can be complete.

review_response.action: kept because ENISA states no outcome; all IMP-* rows are D-UNDESCRIBED with a reason naming the generic wording (same rule as TR37 and TR35). The threat is labelled entry-only in the notes.

review_response.finding: IA-0012 quote is about transient devices while ENISA names production machinery; IA-0001.03 sent to TR55 with 'TR58 is about access'
review_response.action: fixed: IA-0012 keeps the vector quote 'machinery in production/assembly facilities or launch facility' with a SPARTA quote about EGSE and test equipment. IA-0001.* stay D-OTHER TR55 with reasons that state the split: TR55 is how a component is altered, TR58 states no alteration, only access.

review_response.finding: IA-0011 (auxiliary devices) is not a candidate although 'physical devices' is the ENISA phrase
review_response.action: fixed: IA-0011 is now a candidate and coded D-UNDESCRIBED, because ENISA's devices are the machines that are accessed, not media loaded into a spacecraft.

review_response.finding: fix pass m8: IA-0007 and IA-0012 coded K-ACTION here but K-ENABLE in other threats

rows.enisa_quote: Unauthorized access to physical devices in scope of the satellite lifecycle, such as physical workstations
rows.sparta_quote: Compromising the ground segment gives an adversary the most direct path to first execution against a spacecraft
rows.reason: ENISA names unauthorized access to physical workstations, which is the foothold in the mission's ground systems; ENISA lists no follow-on activity, so the chain ends at the entry.

rows.enisa_quote: machinery in production/assembly facilities or launch facility
rows.sparta_quote: Test controllers, EGSE, simulators, flatsats, loaders, and data recorders connect to the same buses and command paths that will exist on orbit
rows.reason: ENISA names machinery in production, assembly and launch facilities and lists EGSE/MGSE among the assets; SPARTA's ATLO technique is abuse of exactly that test and integration equipment.
Inserting malicious artifacts into delivered components is the supply chain compromise ENISA TR55 describes; TR58 names unauthorized use of the machinery and no artifact it alters.
Tainting dependencies and build tools is the open-source and tooling compromise ENISA TR55 names; TR58 names equipment access, not what is changed through it.
Delivering altered software through a third party is what ENISA TR55 describes; TR58 states no software delivery.

SPARTA lists programming stations and golden images as hardware-tampering leverage, but ENISA TR58 states no modification; a hardware component altered before delivery is the TR55 clause on backdoors in third parties' components.
Compromise of a software-defined radio is not named; ENISA's devices are workstations and production machinery.
Reaching a satellite over a crosslink is not described; TR58 is about ground and production devices.
A secondary or backup channel is not mentioned.
Targeting backup ground stations during failover is not described; ENISA names physical devices in general.
A receiver foothold is not mentioned.
Rendezvous and proximity operations act on a satellite in orbit; ENISA's devices are on the ground.
Emanations collection from a nearby spacecraft is not described.
Docked-vehicle access is on-orbit; ENISA's devices are ground-based.
Grappling a satellite is a proximity attack; ENISA's devices are ground-based.
A hosted payload is not mentioned.
Tampering with the on-orbit update pipeline is one possible activity; ENISA does not name updates.
Sending commands through a valid ground station is the malicious commanding ENISA TR52 describes; TR58 gives the access, not commanding.
An outside RF transmitter is not described; the attacker is at a physical device.
A rogue ground station is not described; the attacker uses an existing mission device.
A rogue spacecraft is not described.
A counterspace weapon is not described.
Riding a trusted partner connection is not described; the access is physical.
A mission collaborator is not mentioned.
Vendor routes into operations are the supplier compromise ENISA TR55 describes; TR58 names unauthorized access to the devices themselves, not a vendor.
User-segment access is not described.
Timing access to safe mode is not described.

Auxiliary-device compromise abuses peripherals or media that a spacecraft or its support equipment ingests; ENISA's physical devices are the workstations and machinery that are accessed, not media loaded into the vehicle.
Using a host spacecraft to reach a hosted payload is not described.
Invoking native spacecraft functions is one possible activity: ENISA says only 'multitude of nefarious activities'; no outcome is named, so no impact is kept.
A forced state or mode change is not named: ENISA says only 'multitude of nefarious activities'; no outcome is named, so no impact is kept.
A change to settings or tables is not named: ENISA says only 'multitude of nefarious activities'; no outcome is named, so no impact is kept.
Altering data is not named: ENISA says only 'multitude of nefarious activities'; no outcome is named, so no impact is kept.
Manipulating command or data flow is not named: ENISA says only 'multitude of nefarious activities'; no outcome is named, so no impact is kept.
Altering firmware or programmable logic is not named: ENISA says only 'multitude of nefarious activities'; no outcome is named, so no impact is kept.
Resource exhaustion is not named: ENISA says only 'multitude of nefarious activities'; no outcome is named, so no impact is kept.
Timing or synchronisation manipulation is not named: ENISA says only 'multitude of nefarious activities'; no outcome is named, so no impact is kept.
Pivoting from a hosted payload to the bus is not described.
Hopping between satellites over crosslinks is not described.
